title: Erra and Ishum, Tablet I: Erra roused to war
source: British Museum tablet photographs + eBL manuscript transliterations (eBL corpus edition L I.5, Erra and Ishum, SB I) + English of the eBL edition (B. R. Foster (eBL edition))
description: Erra and Ishum, Tablet I: 134 of 191 lines, each shown on a photographed cuneiform tablet (8 tablets), with the eBL transliteration of that tablet and B. R. Foster's English translation.
introduction:
After a hymn to Ishum, the poem shows Erra lying idle. The Seven, his weapons, urge him to war. Erra goes to Babylon and persuades Marduk to leave his dwelling so that his insignia may be cleaned, promising to keep order while he is away.

Erra and Ishum, written on five tablets by Kabti-ilani-Marduk (probably 8th century BCE), tells how Erra, god of war and plague, persuades Marduk to leave his throne and then devastates Babylonia, until his vizier Ishum calms him. Copies of the poem were used as amulets against plague. The eBL edition so far covers Tablet I only. This page follows the line numbering of the electronic Babylonian Library edition.

How this page is built. Each section is a run of consecutive lines as written on one photographed clay tablet. For every line the eBL edition (https://www.ebl.lmu.de/corpus/L/1/5/SB/I) lists the manuscripts that carry it, with each tablet's own column and line numbers; the tablet chosen for each run is the photographed manuscript with the most signs preserved there. The original text is eBL's transliteration of that tablet's signs (not a modern composite text): square brackets mark broken signs, x an illegible sign, # a damaged sign, ? an uncertain reading, and words in {braces} are determinatives. Superscript numbers are the line numbers of the eBL edition, used in both the Akkadian and the English. The English is B. R. Foster's translation in the eBL edition (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0), one line of English per line of the text; italics mark uncertain renderings, as in the source.

Finding a line on the photograph. Each section names the tablet, the face and column, and the tablet's own line numbers (a prime, as in 5', counts from the first preserved line of a broken column). On a tablet with six columns the obverse carries columns i-iii from left to right; the reverse, turned over from bottom to top, carries columns iv-vi from right to left. The photographs often show the obverse above the reverse with the edges around them; a fragment preserves only part of this layout.

This page shows 134 of the 191 lines of the eBL edition (70%), from 8 tablets in the British Museum: BM.35931, BM.36197, K.8571 (Nineveh), K.16694 (Nineveh), BM.36974, BM.37217, K.10023 (Nineveh), K.13361 (Nineveh).

Lines not shown. 57 of the 191 lines of the eBL edition have no witness here with an open photograph: 20-27 (only on VAT.9162, SU-1951.122); 28-29 (only on VAT.9162, IM.95180, SU-1951.122, IM.74442); 30 (only on VAT.9162, IM.95180, SU-1951.122); 31-33 (only on VAT.9162, SU-1951.122); 86-91 (only on VAT.9162, SU-1951.122); 117-120 (only on SU-1951.122); 121-125 (only on SU-1951.122, VAT.10174); 126-129 (only on SU-1951.122, VAT.9162, VAT.10174); 166-176 (only on VAT.9162, IM.95180, SU-1951.122); 177-180 (only on VAT.9162, SU-1951.122); 183-191 (only on VAT.9162, SU-1951.122). Lines that survive only on tablets whose photographs are not openly licensed (for example in the Iraq Museum, Berlin, Istanbul, Ankara, Philadelphia or private collections), or only on tablets whose eBL photograph does not show the lines, are omitted.
translator_notes: Akkadian: eBL transliteration of the signs on the photographed tablet (manuscript-level ATF), not a composite text.
English: B. R. Foster's translation in the eBL edition; it renders eBL's composite text, including restorations from other tablets.
Line numbers: eBL edition. Each section also gives the tablet's own column and line numbers.

translation.text:
1King of all settlements, creator of the universe, […]!
2Hendursanga, first-born son of Enlil, [...],
3Bearer of the august scepter, shepherd of the black-headed people, herdsman of [mankind]!
4Išum, zealous butcher whose hands are suited to bear his fierce weapons,
5And at the lightning of whose wrathful spears even Erra, the warrior of the gods, trembles in (his) abode!
translation.scan_note: British Museum BM.35931: column i, the tablet's own lines 1 to 5. eBL's corpus edition (https://www.ebl.lmu.de/corpus/L/1/5/SB/I) attributes SB I 1-5 to this manuscript at these column and line numbers. Photograph checked: obverse, reverse and edges of a fragment about 3 cm wide, ink 35931 on two edges. About 10 lines of small script on the obverse and a blank reverse, consistent with eBL's column i (8). eBL treats BM.35931 + Sp-III.855 as one manuscript and holds a separate photograph of each of these pieces; it does not say which piece carries which line, so all of these photographs are linked, and the lines are on one or more of them. The English translates eBL's composite text: words in square brackets are restored, partly from other manuscripts, and may not be legible on this tablet.

translation.text:
6His heart yearned for combat;
7To his weapons he exhorted, “Smear yourselves with deadly venom!”
8To the Seven, peerless warriors, “Gird your arms!”
9And he said to you, (Išum): “I shall head for the (battle) field!”
10You alone are the torch, it is your light they look to!
11You alone are the champion, the gods [march behind!]
12You alone are the sword, the butcher […]!
13Should Erra arise, when he destroys the country,
14Your mind will not rejoice, your heart will not be joyous.
15Erra, like a sleepless man, his limbs are weary,
16To his heart he said: “Shall I arise? Or shall I sleep on?”
17To his weapons he exhorted, “Keep leaning on the corners!”
18To the Seven, peerless warriors, “Return to your abode!”.
19Until you should wake him, he is asleep in his bed,

translation.text:
34He exhorted the third: “Let your face be that of a lion so that whoever beholds you melts down!”
35He said to the fourth: “May the mountain be destroyed at the attack of your fiery weapons!”
36And then to the fifth he said: “Blow like the wind and overwhelm the world!”
37To the sixth he commanded: “sweep over above and below, sparing no one!”
38The seventh he filled with viper’s venom: “Finish (all) life!”.
39Once Anu had fixed the lot of all Seven,
40He handed them over to Erra, the warrior of the gods, (saying): “Let them march at your flank!
41“When the noise of the peoples in settlements becomes unbearable to you,
42“And your temper drives you to decimate them,
43“To ravage the black-headed and the wild beasts to destroy,
44“Let these be your wrathful weapons, that they march at your flank!”.
45They are furious, their weapons are raised,
46They turn to Erra: “Rise! Stand up!
47“Why, like a worn-out old man, do you reside in a city,
48“Like a little child do you reside in a house?
49“As one who knows not the (battle) field, will we eat the bread of women?
50“As if we did not know how to fight, should we tremble and fear?
51“Going to the (battle) field is becoming for manhood, like a festival!
52“The city dweller, be he a prince, bread does not satiate him,
53“Criticized by his own people, despised,
54“He will have to beg to the humblest soldier.
55“The city dweller, however mighty his strength,
56“In what does it advantage the humblest soldier?
57“The abundant bread of the city cannot compare with the cake baked in embers!
58“The fine, honeyed beer cannot compare with the water from a waterskin!

translation.text:
59“The palace on the citadel cannot compare with the shepherd’s hut!
60“Warrior Erra, go out into the (battle) field, rattle your weapons!
61“Make your noise loud, so that those above and below tremble!
62“Let the Igigi hear it and extol your name!
63“Let the Anunnaki hear it and fear the mention of you!
64“Let the gods hear it and bend for your yoke!
65“Let the kings hear it and kneel before you!
66“Let the countries hear it and bring you their tribute!
67“Let the demons hear it and die for themselves!
68“Let the mighty one hear it and diminish his strength!
69“Let the tall mountains hear it and be destroyed, and their summits be leveled!
70“Let the rolling seas hear it and be troubled, and destroy (their) fauna!
71“From the thickest forests let its trunks be uprooted!
72“In the impenetrable reed-bed, let its reeds be snapped!
73“May the peoples fear and their noise be quieted!
74“Let the wild beasts shake and be brought to dust!
75“May your fathers the gods regard and praise your heroism!
76“Warrior Erra, why have you forsaken the (battle) field and reside in the city?
77“The wild cattle and the wild beasts have despised us.
78“Erra warrior, to you we address ourselves: Let our speech be unberable to you!
79“Before the whole country belittles us,
80“You must surely hear our advice!
81“Do a kindness to the Anunnaki, who love silence:
82“The Anunnaki, because of the noise of the people, are unable to fall asleep.
83“The pastures – the source of life of the country – are trodden by cattle.
84“The farmer, over his land, weeps bitterly.
85“The lion and the wolf destroy the wild cattle.

translation.text:
92Warrior Erra heard them,
93The words of the Seven pleased him like the finest of oils.
94He prepared to speak, addressing Išum:
95“Why, having heard this, are you sitting silent?
96“Open the path, I shall take to the road!
97“Let the Seven, the peerless warriors, make war!
98“Make my fierce weapons march to my flank!
99“And you, my champion, come before me!”.
100[When] Išum [heard] these words,
101Moved with compassion he said, [“alas!”]
102“Warrior Erra, why have you devised insidious plots against the gods?
103“You have plotted to ravage the earth and destroy [its inhabitants]; will you not desist?”
104Erra prepared to speak,
105Addressing Išum, his champion, in these words:
106“Išum, pay attention, listen to my words!
107“Concerning the peoples in settlements, whose pardon you requested,
108“O champion of the gods, wise Išum, whose counsel is sweet!
109“In heaven I am a wild bull, on earth I am a lion,
110“In the land I am a king, among the gods a fury,
111“Among the Igigi I am a hero, among the Anunnaki a champion,
112“Among the beasts I am a bowhunter, in the mountain the pit-trap,
113“In the reedbed I am the fire, in the forest the axe,
114“In campaign I am the standard,
115“As the wind I blow, as Adad I thunder;
116“Like the sun god I oversee the whole orb.

130To Erra, the warrior of the gods, he addressed (his) word:
131“Warrior Erra! Regarding that action you suggested:
132“Once, in my anger, I arose from my throne, causing a flood;
133“I arose from my residence, and the seams of heaven and earth were rent asunder.
134“The heavens that were shaken: (for this cause,) the celestial bodies changed their positions, and I did not restore them to their places;
135“The netherworld that trembled: (for this cause,) the (production) of the furrow decreased to such an extent that it was forever difficult to levy (taxes on it);

translation.text:
136“The seams of heaven and earth that were rent asunder: the springs diminished and the floods receded. When I looked again, it was scarcely enough.
137“The progeny of the living beings was scarce, but I did not restore things;
138“Till, like a farmer, I took their seedlings in my hand.
139“I built a(nother) house and settled therein.
140“My image, which by reason of the deluge was removed, whose appearance was tarnished;
141“I ordered the fire god to polish my face and cleanse my garments.
142“When he had polished my image and fulfilled the action,
143“And I had girded on the diadem of my lordship and returned to my place,
144“My countenance was haughty, terrifying was my glance!
145“The people that escaped the flood saw the action fulfilled:
146“If I should now lift up my weapons, I would destroy the rest.
147“Those craftsmen I brought down to the Apsû, and I have not yet decreed their return,
148“I changed the location of the mēsu-tree (and its) amber, and revealed it to none.

translation.text:
149“Now about that action you mentioned, O hero Erra!
150“Where is the mēsu-tree, the flesh of the gods, fitting for the king of the universe?
151“The pure tree, the splendid lad, which is meet for lordship;
152“That in the waters of the vast sea spreads its roots a hundred double-hours to reach the depths of the Netherworld;
153“Whose top in the heights touches the sky of Anu?

translation.text:
154“Where is the pure blue pigment that was made (as) splendid (as) lapis lazuli?
155“Where is Ninildu, master carpenter of my sovereignty?
156“Bearer of the pure golden axe, skilled in the (carving of) that tree (scil. the mēsu-tree),
157“Who makes (it) shine like the noonday and places (it) at my feet?
158“Where is Kusibanda, the creator (of the images) of god and men, whose hands are choice?
159“Where is Ninagal, the bearer of the upper and lower millstones,
160“Who molds strong copper as (easily as) leather, the inventor of in[struments]?
